A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the modern Earth, the terrestrial Ni isotopic cycle is dominated by the processes of continental weathering, and that the oceans are the primary sink for isotopically heavy Ni.
the isotopic systematics of terrestrial Ni are controlled by the same fundamental chemical reactions that govern the distribution of this trace metal in the near surface environment.

Ni isotope fractionation is a common feature of terrestrial weathering, and that the isotopic composition of dissolved Ni in the oceans may be strongly influenced by the isotopic compositions of Ni in continental weathering products.
The main takeaway from our work is that

Ni isotopes can be used as a tool to understand the biogeochemistry of the trace element Ni, and the processes that govern its distribution in the near surface environment, and in the ocean, where the dissolved pool is derived from weathering of terrestrial rocks.

Ni isotopes can be useful tracers of the chemical and mineralogical evolution of terrestrial weathering environments, which is important for understanding the biogeochemistry of this essential element in the context of the Earth's surface environment.

Ni isotope fractionations in the weathering environment may have been much more complex than previously thought, and that Ni isotope compositions in the terrestrial environment may be much more sensitive to environmental and climatological changes than previously thought.
